latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Viable S. aureus enters blood from skin/soft tissue, catheter, hemodialysis access, bone/joint, pneumonia, postoperative wound, endovascular material, or an initially occult focus.
Density and persistence of live S. aureus in blood; drives culture positivity, inflammatory response, and probability of endovascular or metastatic seeding.
TLR2, complement, neutrophil, monocyte, IL-1/TNF/IL-6 response to circulating S. aureus; produces fever, tachycardia, CRP/procalcitonin rise, leukocyte changes, and sepsis physiology.
S. aureus adhesins bind fibrinogen, fibronectin, platelets, endothelium, catheters, prosthetic valves, grafts, and thrombi; biofilm or vegetation protects organisms and sustains bacteremia.

Retained catheter, infected thrombus, prosthetic material, abscess, gallbladder/biliary nidus, bone/joint focus, or undrained soft tissue collection continues to seed blood despite active antibiotics.

Bloodstream spread to vertebrae, epidural/paraspinal space, joints, kidneys, spleen, brain, eye, muscle, gallbladder, vascular grafts, or other deep sites; risk rises with persistent bacteremia and delayed source control.

Adhesion to native/prosthetic valve or cardiac device with vegetation formation, persistent bacteremia, regurgitation/destruction, and embolic complications; can be present even without a murmur or obvious source.
Distributive shock, endothelial leak, microvascular dysfunction, AKI, ARDS, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, and hypoperfusion from invasive bloodstream infection and host response.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Staphylococcal toxin and virulence factor tissue injury
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Variable expression of alpha-toxin, leukocidins, superantigens, enterotoxins, and immune-evasion factors can amplify tissue necrosis, purpura, rhabdomyolysis, pneumonia, shock, and metastatic damage.

Methicillin resistance, high vancomycin exposure failure, elevated vancomycin MIC, daptomycin non-susceptibility, inadequate dosing, delayed active therapy, or biofilm-protected burden blunts bacteremia clearance.

mechanism_edges.rationale: Entry of viable S. aureus is required before measurable bacteremia burden exists.
Higher viable burden raises probability and speed of blood culture positivity.
Bacterial load reflects viable organisms in blood.
Uncleared bloodstream burden creates persistent positive follow-up cultures.
Circulating S. aureus rapidly activates innate immune pathways.
Sustained bacteremia increases opportunity for adhesion to thrombus, valve, catheter, or prosthetic material.
Longer and higher bacteremia burden increases probability of deep metastatic infection.
IL-1/TNF/IL-6 response produces fever, though fever may be blunted in elderly or immunosuppressed patients.
Fever, catecholamines, pain, and sepsis physiology drive tachycardia.
Leukocytosis is common, but severe sepsis, marrow disease, or immunosuppression may blunt or lower WBC.
Neutrophilia is the typical myeloid response to invasive S. aureus.
CRP rises substantially in invasive bacterial infection and deep foci.
Bacterial bloodstream infection and septic organ dysfunction often raise procalcitonin.
Platelets can fall from sepsis consumption, DIC-like coagulopathy, or severe inflammatory illness.
Distributive shock lowers MAP.
Septic vasodilation and capillary leak cause hypotension.
Metabolic acidosis, shock, pneumonia, or ARDS increase respiratory drive.
ARDS, septic pulmonary emboli, pneumonia, or fluid overload can lower saturation.
Shock and tissue hypoperfusion raise lactate.
Sepsis-associated AKI and renal hypoperfusion raise creatinine.
AKI and catabolic stress raise BUN.
Sepsis-associated encephalopathy, shock, or CNS embolic/metastatic disease alters mental status.
Organ dysfunction and hypotension are the immediate pathway to septic shock.
Shock, nephrotoxic therapy, and inflammatory kidney injury increase AKI risk.
Sepsis and lung involvement can progress to ARDS.
Intravascular biofilm and catheter colonization create catheter-source SAB.
Infected thrombus can form around catheters or damaged veins and sustain bacteremia.
S. aureus endovascular adhesion is the bridge from SAB to valve/device infection.
Retained focus continues to reseed blood until removed or drained.
Persistent or deep foci increase the need for device removal, drainage, or surgery.
Longer uncontrolled bacteremia increases metastatic seeding.
Metastatic seeding manifests as radiographic or clinical deep foci.
Hematogenous vertebral osteomyelitis is a classic SAB metastatic complication.
Deep seeded sites can mature into abscesses or phlegmon requiring drainage.
Persistent SAB raises risk of vertebral seeding and epidural/paraspinal extension.
Valve/device infection risk increases with persistent or community-acquired SAB.
Active pathway produces echocardiographic or clinical IE evidence.
Vegetation size is an imaging expression of the endocarditis pathway.
Vegetations and infected endovascular thrombi can embolize to systemic or pulmonary circulation.
Toxin/vascular injury and severe sepsis can produce petechiae, purpura, or necrotic vasculitic lesions.
Severe staphylococcal sepsis, myositis, or toxin-mediated muscle injury may cause rhabdomyolysis.
Shock liver, muscle injury, or toxin-mediated tissue injury can raise AST.
Hepatic injury can accompany severe SAB and shock.
Inactive, underdosed, or failing therapy prolongs positive cultures.
Resistance or non-activity prevents bacterial burden decline.
High/persistent SAB burden is associated with complications and death.
Shock, AKI, ARDS, and encephalopathy are immediate mortality drivers.
Deep metastatic foci prolong infection and add neurologic, embolic, and source-control hazards.

axes.shape_free_text: Fever is common but may be absent or low-grade in older adults, ESRD, immunosuppression, or after antipyretics/antibiotics.
Tachycardia tracks fever, pain, catecholamine tone, and shock.
Rises with sepsis, metabolic acidosis, pneumonia, pulmonary embolic disease, or ARDS.
Often preserved in isolated bacteremia; falls with pneumonia, septic pulmonary emboli, ARDS, pulmonary edema, or severe shock.
Normal in uncomplicated SAB; low in septic shock or high/variable during neurologic catastrophe.
Falls with distributive shock; vasopressors and fluids may normalize it despite high disease activity.
Often neutrophilic leukocytosis; may be normal or low in elderly, ESRD, marrow disease, immunosuppression, or fulminant sepsis.
Neutrophilia is typical when marrow reserve is intact.
Normal or elevated in inflammation; thrombocytopenia with severe sepsis, DIC-like coagulopathy, liver dysfunction, or marrow stress.
May be normal early; anemia is common with chronic disease, ESRD, endocarditis, hemolysis, bleeding, or prolonged hospitalization.
Often markedly elevated, especially with deep infection or osteomyelitis; declines after active therapy and source control.
Variable but can be high in SAB sepsis; not a species-specific diagnostic test.
Usually normal in uncomplicated SAB; elevated with shock, hypoperfusion, or severe respiratory failure.
Rises with sepsis-associated AKI, underlying CKD/ESRD, renal emboli, nephrotoxic therapy, or rhabdomyolysis.
Rises with AKI, ESRD, hypoperfusion, catabolic state, or dehydration.
Mild to marked rise from shock liver, muscle injury/rhabdomyolysis, biliary focus, or drug toxicity.
Mild to marked rise from hepatic injury, shock, biliary involvement, or drug toxicity.
Usually normal or mildly elevated; rises with biliary or hepatic involvement.
Usually normal; rises with cholestasis, hepatic dysfunction, hemolysis, or severe sepsis.
Usually normal; can be high with staphylococcal myositis, rhabdomyolysis, shock, or daptomycin toxicity.
Disorientation, delirium, obtundation, coma, or encephalopathy from sepsis, shock, CNS emboli, hemorrhage, or metastatic infection.
May be systemic inflammatory myalgia, focal pyomyositis, or rhabdomyolysis-associated pain.
Can be nonspecific inflammatory arthralgia or clue to septic arthritis/metastatic infection.
Petechiae/purpura may reflect embolic lesions, vasculitic lesions, DIC-like sepsis, thrombocytopenia, or toxin-mediated vascular injury.
Clinical context axis for follow-up culture probability; organism identification is confirmatory evidence and should not be treated as ordinary presentation evidence.
Approximate bacterial load/time-to-positivity correlate; not usually available as a routine numeric value.
Duration of documented follow-up blood culture positivity after index culture or active therapy; use as clinical-course context, not as species-identification ordinary evidence.
MRSA vs MSSA context; must come from microbiology/epidemiologic risk, not vitals alone.
Probability that nafcillin/oxacillin/cefazolin has active anti-staphylococcal effect; high in MSSA, low in MRSA.
Probability of microbiologic vancomycin activity, distinct from clinical adequacy in MSSA, high-inoculum, biofilm, or elevated-MIC disease.
Probability of daptomycin activity; can fall with de novo non-susceptibility or prior glycopeptide/daptomycin exposure.
Probability of ceftaroline activity against MRSA/MSSA isolate; used mainly as active beta-lactam context or combination/salvage context.
Probability that an intravascular catheter is the primary or sustaining source.
Probability that a catheter itself is infected or culture-positive.
Central venous catheter, hemodialysis catheter, port, vascular graft/stent, pacemaker/ICD lead, or other intravascular material.
Hemodialysis catheter, AV graft, AV fistula, or recent dialysis access manipulation.
Prosthetic valve, vascular graft/stent, orthopedic hardware, prosthetic joint, or other implanted material vulnerable to S. aureus biofilm.
Probability that cellulitis, abscess, wound, ulcer, gangrene, or injection-site infection is the portal/source.
Need for catheter/device removal, abscess drainage, debridement, valve surgery, thrombectomy, or other focus control.
Completeness of source control; high means infected line/material removed and drainable foci controlled.

Any deep hematogenous focus: vertebral osteomyelitis, epidural/paraspinal phlegmon/abscess, septic arthritis, splenic/renal/brain abscess, endophthalmitis, gallbladder focus, or infected graft/thrombus.
MRI/CT/biopsy evidence of vertebral osteomyelitis, spondylodiscitis, or contiguous paraspinal/epidural inflammatory focus.
Imaging evidence of infected venous thrombus, catheter-associated thrombus, or septic thrombophlebitis.
Echo, intracardiac device, or clinical evidence that SAB has complicated into infective endocarditis; use as complication/context, not as the disease name.
Vegetation size if SAB-associated endocarditis is present.
Risk of requiring vasopressors or meeting septic shock physiology.
Risk of AKI from shock, nephrotoxicity, renal emboli, rhabdomyolysis, or baseline CKD/ESRD stress.
Risk of ARDS from severe sepsis, pneumonia, pulmonary septic emboli, or capillary leak.
Risk that SAB has or develops valve/device endocarditis, especially with persistent bacteremia, community acquisition, prosthetic valves/devices, or no clear source.
Risk of deep abscess/phlegmon or occult seeded focus requiring imaging and drainage.
Risk of hematogenous vertebral osteomyelitis, spondylodiscitis, or epidural/paraspinal extension.
Risk of septic emboli from valve vegetations or infected thrombi to brain, lung, spleen, kidney, skin, or extremities.
Low-frequency but catastrophic hazard from mycotic aneurysm rupture, hemorrhagic transformation, anticoagulation, thrombocytopenia, or coagulopathy.
Lifespan outcome hazard driven by shock, persistent bacteremia, inadequate source control, endocarditis, metastatic infection, AKI/ARDS, age, comorbidity, and inactive therapy.
Nonspecific systemic inflammatory marker that commonly rises in clinically significant pulmonary, metastatic, or disseminated infection; included through horizontal fairness audit.
S. aureus metastatic CNS infection, meningitis, spinal epidural inflammatory extension, or myelitis risk/activity.
Focal weakness, sensory level, gait ataxia, myelopathy, radiculopathy, or other neurologic deficit from metastatic infection or CNS involvement.
CSF pleocytosis when S. aureus bacteremia seeds meninges or causes adjacent spinal inflammatory involvement.
CSF protein elevation from bacterial meningitis, myelitis, or spinal inflammatory block in metastatic S. aureus infection.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fever and tachycardia co-vary after accounting for cytokine drive.
Hypotension and lactate elevation co-move in shock physiology.
Removing infected lines or draining foci shortens bacteremia persistence.
Persistent SAB is a major signal for endocarditis or an endovascular nidus.
The longer SAB persists, the higher the risk of occult deep seeded infection.
SAB-associated vegetations and valve infection can embolize.
Septic cerebral emboli can cause hemorrhagic transformation or mycotic aneurysm rupture.
AKI and renal replacement needs increase mortality and treatment toxicity constraints.
ARDS is a major organ-failure mortality pathway in SAB sepsis.
A drainable or removable uncontrolled focus worsens outcome until controlled.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Microbiologic susceptibility is required for organism killing.
MRSA probability increases the need for MRSA-active coverage.
For confirmed MSSA, anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam activity clears bacteremia more reliably than vancomycin.
Requires AUC-guided dosing and nephrotoxicity monitoring.
Vancomycin cannot reliably sterilize retained infected material or undrained abscesses alone.

failure_modes: MSSA treated without active beta-lactam when beta-lactam can be given
elevated vancomycin MIC or clinical non-response
retained catheter, thrombus, valve/device vegetation, or abscess
subtherapeutic exposure or nephrotoxicity limiting exposure

side_effects.interpretation: Nephrotoxicity risk, especially with AKI, high exposure, or concurrent nephrotoxins.

treatments.context_specific_role: MRSA-active bactericidal therapy and empiric coverage when MRSA probability is clinically meaningful.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cefazolin is bactericidal for susceptible MSSA bloodstream infection.
MRSA is not reliably treated by cefazolin.
Severe beta-lactam allergy may preclude cephalosporin therapy.

failure_modes: MRSA
severe beta-lactam allergy
high-inoculum deep infection with inadequate source control
unrecognized endocarditis or metastatic abscess
treatments.context_specific_role: Bactericidal anti-staphylococcal beta-lactam therapy when the isolate is methicillin-susceptible and allergy context allows.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Oxacillin/nafcillin are bactericidal for MSSA.
MRSA is resistant to anti-staphylococcal penicillins.
Immediate penicillin hypersensitivity can preclude use or require desensitization context.
Severe cutaneous or anaphylactic beta-lactam reaction limits use.

failure_modes: MRSA
severe penicillin allergy
hepatic toxicity or interstitial nephritis
retained focus or endocarditis requiring source control/surgery

side_effects.interpretation: Hepatic enzyme elevation can occur during prolonged anti-staphylococcal penicillin therapy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Bactericidal therapy for methicillin-susceptible SAB when allergy and toxicity context allow.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Daptomycin requires isolate susceptibility.
Daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant and is not suitable for primary pneumonia.
Baseline or rising CK increases myopathy monitoring concern.

failure_modes: daptomycin non-susceptibility
primary pneumonia focus
persistent biofilm/infected thrombus without source control
myopathy or eosinophilic pneumonia toxicity
treatments.context_specific_role: Bactericidal MRSA-active or beta-lactam-intolerant SAB therapy when pulmonary focus is not dominant and susceptibility is retained.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Ceftaroline activity depends on isolate susceptibility.
Ceftaroline retains PBP2a activity for many MRSA isolates.
Severe beta-lactam reaction limits cephalosporin use.
Clinical use often arises when persistent MRSA bacteremia requires an active beta-lactam component.

failure_modes: severe beta-lactam allergy
ceftaroline non-susceptibility
retained source or endovascular focus
neutropenia with prolonged exposure

side_effects.interpretation: Neutropenia can occur with prolonged ceftaroline.

treatments.context_specific_role: MRSA-active beta-lactam option, including persistent bacteremia contexts when susceptibility and allergy context permit.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Bacteriostatic activity is less reliable for high-burden endovascular SAB.
Good lung penetration can matter when SAB is linked to MRSA pneumonia.
Linezolid can worsen thrombocytopenia during prolonged therapy.

failure_modes: high-burden endocarditis or retained infected material
bacteriostatic effect insufficient for persistent bacteremia
thrombocytopenia, serotonin toxicity, neuropathy with prolonged use

side_effects.interpretation: Thrombocytopenia risk, especially with prolonged therapy or renal dysfunction.

treatments.context_specific_role: Contextual MRSA-active protein-synthesis inhibitor when tissue penetration or toxin suppression matters, but not a stand-alone solution for high-burden endovascular persistence.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Only cases with removable/drainable foci benefit directly.
Line removal can promptly reduce catheter-associated bloodstream seeding.
Drainage/debridement of deep foci shortens persistence and complication risk.

failure_modes: no drainable or removable focus identified
incomplete drainage or retained prosthetic material
procedure not feasible because of anatomy or instability
new metastatic focus not yet detected

side_effects.interpretation: Drainage, surgery, catheter removal, or thrombectomy can add procedure bleeding risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Removal or drainage of the sustaining nidus: infected catheter, abscess, gallbladder focus, septic thrombus, prosthetic material, or debridable tissue.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hemodynamic push is relevant when shock physiology is present or imminent.
Fluid strategy must be constrained by cardiac and renal reserve.

failure_modes: does not reduce bacterial burden
fluid overload in ESRD/heart failure
persistent shock if active therapy/source control delayed

side_effects.interpretation: Excess crystalloid can worsen pulmonary edema in susceptible patients.

treatments.context_specific_role: State support for shock while antimicrobials and source control reshape the disease process.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises catheter-source and endovascular biofilm probability; renal baseline may be abnormal and should be handled by background/risk context.
Raises endovascular persistence and source-control complexity.
Raises portal probability and, with injection drug use, right-sided endocarditis risk.
Persistence is not a subtype; it signals source-control failure, endovascular infection, resistance, or metastatic focus.

present.treatment_effect_modulation: Makes non-MRSA beta-lactams inactive and shifts effect to MRSA-active agents if susceptible.

present.trajectory_modulation: Prolongs burden and increases metastatic/endovascular seeding opportunities.
Can blunt fever/WBC response while increasing organ failure and mortality hazards.
Raises invasive infection and complication risk; CKD affects renal labs as host background.
Lack of a source should increase search intensity for endocarditis and deep foci rather than reduce disease likelihood.

supportive_care.clinical_rationale: Follow-up cultures define clearance kinetics and expose persistent bacteremia requiring source search.
SAB carries substantial endocarditis risk, especially with persistence, no source, prosthetic material, or embolic signs.
MRI, CT, PET/CT, tagged WBC scan, or symptom-directed imaging can reveal occult abscess, osteomyelitis, infected thrombus, or biliary/other focus.
Vancomycin, daptomycin, beta-lactams, and adjuncts require dose/toxicity monitoring in AKI, CKD, and hemodialysis.
Fluids, vasopressors, oxygen/ventilation, renal replacement therapy, and ICU care support state variables while infection control takes effect.
Specialist review improves detection of complications, antibiotic tailoring, treatment duration, and source-control timing.
